title: Signal-to-noise sweep and routing probes for quantized kernels
content:
Purpose:

Quick experimental notes and early results from a signal-to-noise style sweep to help decide routing heuristics for quantized kernel variants (INT8 / FP8 / GPTQ / AWQ). Goal is actionable guidance for the scheduler: when to prefer a lower-precision kernel for cost, and when to route to a higher-fidelity kernel because quality regressions are visible in the metric signal.

Background / motivation:
- We have multiple kernel implementations for the same model shapes: throughput-optimized (packed lanes, fused kernels) vs fidelity-optimized (higher precision accumulation, slower vectorization).
- Operators configured as kernel variants sometimes show identical macro throughput but diverge in rare prompt patterns (attention spikes, long context prefix reuse).
- We need a lightweight routing policy that uses runtime signals to pick kernels per-request or per-route without heavy evaluator runs. This doc explores simple SNR-like metrics derivable from logits / softmax skew / per-token entropy to predict observable quality regressions.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Requests with high softmax entropy or low next-token confidence are more sensitive to quantization noise.
2) Presence of long repeated prefixes (high KV reuse) reduces sensitivity because error amortizes; therefore prefer throughput kernels.
3) Abrupt attention spikes (long-distance attention patterns) amplify quantization error; prefer fidelity kernels.

Experiment setup (short):
- Models: Llama-2-13B (ops-normal), Llama-2-70B trimmed for throughput simulation (substituted by 30B proxy), and a 7B-family instruct model for quick iterations.
- Quant schemes: INT8 (per-channel symmetric), FP8 (E4M3), GPTQ (8-bit clustered), AWQ (per-block 4-bit-ish style but used in 8-bit fallback config).
- Kernel variants: fast-packed (throughput), conservative-accum (fidelity), hybrid (dynamic block-sizes).
- Hardware: single A100-80GB, batch=1 latency focus; p95 measured from simulated client harness.
- Test corpus: 2k prompts sampled across: short instructions, long-context multi-turns, synthetic attention-spike prompts (rare tokens at long positions), and OpenWebText random slices for language modeling perplexity.
- Quality metrics: delta-logprob (avg next-token logprob vs fp32 baseline), coh-score (embedding cosine between quantized vs fp32 completion), downstream MMLU micro-accuracy for a subset, and subjective short-list manual triage for unexpected modes.

Signals computed in-harness (cheap, online):
- top1_conf = softmax(max) per-next-token (scalar)
- entropy = -sum(p * log p) for top-K (K=16)
- logprob_drift = (quant_logprob - fp32_logprob) aggregated over first N tokens (N=16)
- kv_reuse_ratio = fraction of tokens that hit cache (simulated by repeating prefixes)
- attention_span_metric = avg attention distance weighted by score mass (cheap approx from attention pattern sketch)
SNR proxy: snr_proxy = mean(top1_conf) / (std(logprob_drift) + epsilon) — larger means stable signal (less sensitive), small means high noise. This is intentionally simple to compute inside runtime.

Representative results (high-level, aggregated):
- Short prompts (<=32 tokens):
  - INT8 fast-packed: throughput +18% vs fidelity kernel, p95 latency improved ~12ms; quality-regret (avg delta-logprob) ~0.6 nats, model MMLU delta ~-0.5% (within noise).
  - FP8 conservative: throughput -8% vs fast-packed, quality-regret ~0.12 nats (much lower).
  - Routing based solely on snr_proxy correctly selected fidelity kernel for ~14% of short prompts where delta-logprob > 0.9 nats.

- Long-context / multi-turn (>512 tokens):
  - KV reuse ratio correlated strongly with tolerance: reuse_ratio > 0.6 => quant kernels rarely induced perceptible drift.
  - In cases with attention spikes (engineered prompts), AWQ showed abrupt per-token instability: local spikes in logprob_drift up to 2.8 nats for 1-3 tokens, then recovered. FP8 handled those spikes best.

- Throughput vs tail-latency tradeoff:
  - Fast-packed kernels increase average tokens/sec by 20-30% under light concurrency but amplify p95 tails when a fidelity fallback is required mid-stream (warmup of higher-fidelity kernel causes 150-300ms penalty).
  - Prefer warm routing decisions (at request start) rather than mid-stream swaps for latency-sensitive routes.

Routing heuristic candidate (runtime-friendly):
- At request start compute: top1_conf_start (avg over first 2 autoregressive tokens), entropy_start, and check kv_reuse_hint from client (if client signals repeating prefix).
- If top1_conf_start < 0.35 OR entropy_start > 3.5 => route to fidelity kernel.
- Else if kv_reuse_hint >= 0.6 => route to throughput kernel.
- Else use snr_proxy threshold: if snr_proxy < 0.9 => fidelity, otherwise throughput.
- Fall back policy: if quant kernel produces catastrophic token (logprob_drift > 2.5 for any token in first 16) then soft-fail: return partial and enqueue a higher-fidelity re-gen async for audit (deferred re-render), and mark route for telemetry.

Observed failure modes / gotchas:
- logprob drift requires baseline fp32 or high-fidelity reference. For production we approximate by comparing to a local higher-precision kernel when available — costy. Need a cheaper proxy (top1_conf / entropy used above).
- Some prompts are adversarially sensitive to minor bit flips (rare). These tend to be long, math-like, or token-misaligned sequences. Signal thresholds need to be conservative to avoid false positives.
- Kernel warmup cost: moving to fidelity kernel mid-request is expensive because caches/allocations change. Prefer start-of-request decisions or amortize by reusing cold fidelity workers with low RT.
- AWQ behavior varies by block-size and layer; it was flaky on some 70B-proxy layers (we saw drift concentrated in early attention layers).

Quick diagnostic checklist (for triage):
- Step 1: reproduce sample with fp32 baseline and quantized kernel; capture per-token logprobs and attention span metric.
- Step 2: if drift concentrated on tokens with low top1_conf or high entropy, mark as SNR-sensitive and consider routing threshold adjustments.
- Step 3: check kv_reuse_ratio; if high, verify drift isn't caused by caching mismatch.
- Step 4: for AWQ/GPTQ variants check per-layer scale distributions and quant noise histograms (PR to add instrumentation if missing).

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we reduce warmup penalty by keeping small pool of standby fidelity workers pinned per-route? Cost/benefit simulation needed.
- How stable are snr_proxy thresholds across model families and sequence lengths? Need cross-model sweep (7B, 13B, 30B proxy, 70B) with controlled prompts.
- Explore lightweight learned classifier (tiny MLP on the 4 cheap signals) to predict whether delta-logprob > 0.7 nats; offline training might outperform static thresholds with minimal runtime cost.
- Investigate hybrid kernels that start in throughput mode and switch attention layers to fidelity selectively (layer-level mixed precision) to reduce warmup.

Notes / TODOs:
- Diego: add per-layer AWQ noise dump in our microprof harness (ticket ENG-1298).
- Sophie: run cross-model threshold sweep for snr_proxy by 2024-11-20 and post results to PR #842.
- Liam: prototype standby fidelity worker pool sim and estimate cost per-1000-requests.

Quick conclusion:
We can derive a cheap runtime signal (snr_proxy + kv_reuse_hint) that correlates sufficiently with observed quality regressions to enable a low-overhead routing heuristic. Conservative thresholds recommended initially to minimize false positives; follow-up work should instrument per-layer quant noise and test a small learned predictor for better sensitivity/precision tradeoffs.
